title: The Day Lakshmi Left
hookLine: a garland tossed to an elephant, and the goddess of fortune leaves the worlds
carry: lakshmi stays where she is honored
tomorrow: lakshmi rises from the churned ocean, and gets to choose

lines: THE KING HANDS IT TO HIS ELEPHANT.
cards: Indra, king of the gods, rides his great white elephant, pleased with himself.
On the road he meets the sage Durvasa, known for his temper, wandering in a wild, ecstatic state with a garland of heavenly flowers on his own head. Durvasa takes it off and throws it up to the king.
Indra catches it and, without really looking, hangs it on the elephant's head. The elephant smells the flowers, takes the garland in its trunk, and throws it on the ground.
That careless moment is where Lakshmi's story begins: the day she left.

teach.h: THE SAGE CURSES THE PROUD KING.
teach.b: The sage sees his garland in the dirt, and his temper breaks. In the Vishnu Purana's telling, he curses Indra: since the king is so swollen with his fortune, his fortune will leave him. And it does.
Shri, the goddess of fortune and prosperity, also called Lakshmi, departs from the three worlds. What follows is quietly frightening. Nobody attacks; nothing explodes.
Things just go dim. In the Purana's description, the plants wither, people stop offering and giving, the gods lose their strength, and the demons start winning. All because one goddess is gone.
So who is Lakshmi as a character? Not a warrior like Durga, not wild like Kali. She is the goddess of everything going well: the full granary, the lamp lit, the house where people are generous.
In the text her leaving is the sage's curse at work, but some retellers draw a trait from it: she doesn't stay where she isn't honored. She isn't cruel about it.
She simply isn't there anymore, and suddenly everyone notices what she was holding together.
That's why, before Diwali, so many Hindu families scrub the house, draw rangoli at the door, and light lamps for Lakshmi puja: they're making a home where Shri is honored, so she'll come in and stay.

teach.h: SHE STAYS WHERE SHE IS HONORED.
teach.b: Some teachers draw the plain lesson: fortune follows reverence, and slips away from arrogance. The story doesn't end in the dark.
To bring her back, the gods will have to do something enormous, together with their enemies. That's tomorrow.

how: Hindus honor Lakshmi in homes and shops, especially at Diwali, and some families keep the house clean and lamps lit in the hope that she will feel welcome and stay.

s: Lakshmi leaves because the demons drive her out
in the Vishnu Purana's telling, she departs after Indra's arrogance with the sage's garland.
when Lakshmi leaves, the worlds go dim rather than explode
plants wither, people stop giving, the gods lose their strength.
Lakshmi is a warrior goddess like Durga
she's the goddess of fortune and things going well; in this story, fortune leaves where it isn't honored.

games.q: you're Indra, riding your elephant. a sage with a well-known temper throws you a garland. what does the story say you do?
o: drop it onto the elephant's head
games.why: Indra drops it on the elephant, which throws it to the ground. Durvasa curses him, and Shri, fortune herself, leaves the three worlds.

practice: At Diwali, many families set small clay lamps at the door so Lakshmi can find her way in.

Tonight, if you can, light a lamp or a candle, or just switch on the light by your door, and as you do, name one good thing in your life you've stopped noticing. Hold it the way Indra should have held the garland, really looking.
If you pray, offer thanks to Lakshmi; if you don't, just say thank you.

wordCard.voice: Durga. The name over this run of five goddesses; today, the run turns to Lakshmi, whose leaving dims the worlds. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Shri, fortune, prosperity, radiance; in the Vishnu Purana's story, the goddess who leaves the worlds.

carryVoice: Your line: lakshmi stays where she is honored. Tomorrow, Lakshmi rises from the ocean. I'll be here tomorrow.
